turns.prompt_text: I would like to make some short script so that I can capture all of my Mac settings in order to quickly reach my current setup point as a checkpoint in case I need to entirely restart my Mac or use a fresh computer entirely. I'm okay with not having everything. I think I should isolate this and separate it into a few chunks. I'm starting with karabiner
turns.response_html:
Isolating this into modular chunks is the absolute best way to build a reliable "dotfiles" or disaster-recovery setup.

For Karabiner-Elements, all your profiles, virtual keyboard settings, and complex modifications live in a single directory: ~/.config/karabiner/. The main file you need is karabiner.json.

Here is a straightforward script strategy to capture this checkpoint and restore it later.

1. The Backup Script (backup.sh)

You can target a centralized directory (like ~/Backup/checkpoint/ or ~/.dotfiles/) to aggregate your configurations.

#!/bin/bash

# Define where you want to pool your configs
BACKUP_DIR="$HOME/.dotfiles/karabiner"
KARABINER_SRC="$HOME/.config/karabiner"

echo "Checking up Karabiner-Elements settings..."

# Create backup directory if it doesn't exist
mkdir -p "$BACKUP_DIR"

# Backup the core configuration file
if [ -f "$KARABINER_SRC/karabiner.json" ]; then
    cp "$KARABINER_SRC/karabiner.json" "$BACKUP_DIR/"
    echo "✓ Core karabiner.json backed up."
else
    echo "✗ Core config not found at $KARABINER_SRC/karabiner.json"
fi

# Backup complex modifications assets if you have any custom/downloaded ones
if [ -d "$KARABINER_SRC/assets" ]; then
    cp -R "$KARABINER_SRC/assets" "$BACKUP_DIR/"
    echo "✓ Complex modifications assets backed up."
fi

echo "Karabiner checkpoint complete!"

2. The Restore Script (restore.sh)

When hitting a fresh machine, installing Karabiner via Homebrew (brew install --cask karabiner-elements) creates the initial directory structure. This snippet safely places your backup files back into position:

#!/bin/bash

BACKUP_DIR="$HOME/.dotfiles/karabiner"
KARABINER_DEST="$HOME/.config/karabiner"

echo "Restoring Karabiner-Elements settings..."

# Ensure target directory exists
mkdir -p "$KARABINER_DEST"

# Restore main json config
if [ -f "$BACKUP_DIR/karabiner.json" ]; then
    cp "$BACKUP_DIR/karabiner.json" "$KARABINER_DEST/"
    echo "✓ Main configuration restored."
else
    echo "✗ No backed up karabiner.json found."
fi

# Restore complex modifications if they exist
if [ -d "$BACKUP_DIR/assets" ]; then
    cp -R "$BACKUP_DIR/assets" "$KARABINER_DEST/"
    echo "✓ Complex modifications assets restored."
fi

# Kickstart the service to ensure Karabiner reloads the files instantly
echo "Restarting Karabiner background agent..."
launchctl kickstart -k gui/$(id -u)/org.pqrs.service.agent.karabiner_console_user_server

echo "Karabiner restore complete!"

Note on Symlinks: If you plan on tracking these configurations via Git in the future, you can transition this script to use symbolic links (ln -s) instead of copying (cp). However, if you symlink the karabiner.json file individually, Karabiner's file watcher sometimes fails to detect updates. It is always safest to symlink the entire parent folder (~/.config/karabiner) rather than just the file.

turns.prompt_text: right now I have turned my entire ~/.config/fish directory into a git repository, doing this helps me keep my state. But I do worry that with updates, the entire thing could become invalid depending on the program.
turns.response_html:
Turning your entire ~/.config/fish directory into a Git repository is a solid way to track state, but your concern is spot-on.

The problem with version-controlling the entire directory is that Fish automatically manages internal state files inside ~/.config/fish. For example, Fish updates files like fish_variables (which stores universal variables) dynamically, and it tracks history or third-party plug-in fragments that change constantly. When Fish updates, or when you move to a new machine, these auto-generated or machine-specific state files can conflict or break things.

The best practice to prevent updates from breaking your configuration is to separate your logic from Fish's system-managed state.

Here is how to bulletproof your setup:

1. Ignore the Dynamic Noise (.gitignore)

You don't want Fish's dynamic run-time state polluting your repository. Add a .gitignore file to the root of your ~/.config/fish/ repo to keep it clean:

# .gitignore inside ~/.config/fish/

# Ignore Fish's auto-generated universal variables file 
# (This often contains machine-specific paths or colors that break on a fresh machine)
fish_variables

# Ignore local history or cache if plugin managers leak them here
.cache/

2. Isolate Machine-Specific Configurations

If you change machines or updates alter environment behaviors, hardcoded paths will bite you. Split your configuration into global logic and local state using a .fish.local file that you don't commit.

At the very end of your ~/.config/fish/config.fish, add this snippet:

# Load a local configuration file if it exists (machine-specific/not tracked in git)
if test -f ~/.config/fish/config.local.fish
    source ~/.config/fish/config.local.fish
end

Then, add config.local.fish to your .gitignore. Use this file for things that change between machines, like specific API keys, hardware-specific paths, or custom experimental aliases.

3. Handle fish_variables Safely

The fish_variables file is the biggest liability because Fish rewrites it constantly. If you want to share specific universal variables across setups (like theme colors or default paths) without tracking the chaotic fish_variables file, explicitly set them as global variables inside your tracked config.fish instead:

# Instead of letting Fish save this universally, hardcode your shared preferences
set -g fish_color_command green --bold
set -g EDITOR nano

By filtering out the dynamic files with a .gitignore and isolating machine-specific paths, your Fish repository will strictly contain your intent (your functions, aliases, and logic) rather than the program's state. This makes it incredibly resilient to software updates and hardware changes.

turns.prompt_text: so my initial approach solution is to have the git repository be one directory deeper, but then there's some friction because the actual config.fish file has to be transported between that directory structure. The option you gave was to just use a.gitignore. This makes a lot of sense.
turns.response_html:
Exactly, the .gitignore approach lets you keep your files exactly where Fish naturally expects them, saving you from writing brittle "transport" or sync scripts that you have to maintain manually.

Keeping a repository one directory deeper (often called a dotfiles folder) is popular, but it relies on creating symbolic links (ln -s) from the repo to your real ~/.config/fish. If you link individual files, it works well, but it adds that layer of friction you noticed. By just initializing Git directly inside ~/.config/fish and using a smart .gitignore, you get the best of both worlds: zero friction and a perfectly clean repository.

To give you a rock-solid starting point, here is a complete, production-ready .gitignore you can drop right into ~/.config/fish/.

# ~/.config/fish/.gitignore

# Ignore Fish's dynamic, auto-generated universal variables file
fish_variables

# Ignore any local, machine-specific overrides
config.local.fish
*.local.fish

# Ignore third-party plugin state/caches if they write to your config dir
.cache/
data/

# Optional: If you use a plugin manager like Fisher, you only need to track the 
# 'fish_plugins' file (which lists what to install) rather than the plugin source code.
# Un-comment the lines below if you want to keep plugin code out of your repo:
# plugins/
# functions/fisher.fish

With this strategy, if you ever need to set up a brand new computer, your recovery process for Fish is elegantly simple:

Pro Tip for Git Cleanliness: Since you already have the repository initialized, after you save your .gitignore, run git rm --cached fish_variables if it was previously tracked. This tells Git to stop watching the file without deleting it from your actual file system.
